name: Smectite (diosmectite, a medicinal clay)
short: Children's trials: constipation was the most reported side effect, not significantly more than control (wide range); no deaths or serious effects. Lead in the medicine not tested in cited sources.
text: Constipation in children: a 2018 Cochrane review of 18 trials (2616 children aged one month to 18 years with acute infectious diarrhoea) found that constipation was the most frequently reported side effect; it did not differ significantly between groups, but the estimate was higher with smectite and very imprecise (risk ratio 4.71, 95% CI 0.56 to 39.19; 2 studies, 128 children; low-certainty evidence), and no deaths or serious adverse effects were reported. A 2015 meta-analysis of 13 placebo-controlled trials (2164 children aged 1 to 60 months) found no increase in the risk of adverse events, and a 2006 meta-analysis of 9 trials (1238 participants) found adverse effects similar in both groups. In single trials in children, no side effects were observed among 804 Italian children treated by primary care paediatricians, and no adverse effects were reported in 117 Indian children aged 2 to 5; in 346 adults with acute watery diarrhoea, the authors describe diosmectite as well tolerated without listing events. Lead: none of the cited sources measured lead or other metals in medicinal smectite, and PubMed searches found no human study of lead in smectite medicines. For other clay products, a 2013 analysis of clays sold for oral use in the Netherlands (traditional clays consumed by pregnant women in Africa, Asia and Suriname and by some immigrants, and clays sold for health purposes; not the smectite medicine) estimated that use of 34 of 36 traditional clays and 2 of 27 health clays would give lead intakes above the toxicological limit, by up to 20-fold, with inorganic arsenic also above its limit for some clays; the authors conclude that lead and arsenic intakes from some clay products could be of concern because of use in pregnancy and possible harm to the developing baby, and discourage their use, especially in pregnancy. Interactions: in healthy volunteers, smectite taken with diazepam lowered diazepam's peak blood level to 91% of the control value and delayed the peak (the abstract says the time to peak was 'prolonged by 153% of the control values'), but did not substantially change phenylbutazone levels; the authors suggest smectite delays the absorption of basic drugs. In a laboratory model of the stomach and duodenum, diosmectite bound more than 81% of fluoroquinolone antibiotics, ranitidine and pyrimethamine, but less than 27% of digoxin and valproic acid. In rats, diosmectite given straight after the cancer medicine osimertinib cut its absorption (area under the curve) by 94%, and by 66% when given 30 minutes later; the authors say clinical studies are needed.
